claim: On YouTube, an average of 85% of all views accrue to a small minority of just 3% of all channels.
scope_conditions: Random sample of YouTube channel and video data spanning approximately 2007-2017 (the paper's 'past 10 years')
quoted_support: It demonstrates stark contrasts between video genres in terms of channels, uploads and views, and that a vast majority of on average 85% of all views goes to a small minority of 3% of all channels.

claim: Older YouTube channels have a significantly higher probability of garnering a large viewership than younger channels.
stance_target: tenure/channel-age is uncorrelated with success (contrasts with Rieder et al. 2020 finding of near-zero correlation between days-active and success)
scope_conditions: Abstract-level claim only; underlying statistical test (regression/correlation coefficient, n, p-value) not accessible in this record
quoted_support: The analytical results give evidence that older channels have a significantly higher probability to garner a large viewership, but also show that there has always been a small chance for young channels to become successful quickly, depending on whether they choose their genre wisely.

claim: Young YouTube channels retain a small but non-zero chance of rapid success, contingent on genre selection.
stance_target: output/strategy (e.g. genre choice) rather than tenure alone determines fast-track success
scope_conditions: Abstract-level claim; genre-specific breakdowns not visible without full text
quoted_support: there has always been a small chance for young channels to become successful quickly, depending on whether they choose their genre wisely

claim: The full text of Baertl (2018) is not accessible via SAGE eprint link, ResearchGate, or the Hochschule Offenburg OPUS institutional repository; all three routes return either a Cloudflare bot-detection block or an abstract-only metadata record.
stance_target: accessibility of primary source for tenure-vs-success on YouTube
